newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Peters to get economic advice by Thursday.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Peters to get economic advice by Thursday.

text.p: New Zealand First leader Winston Peters said he expected to receive independent advice on the state of the economy in time for coalition talks on Thursday.
"We will have those (reports) tomorrow," Peters told reporters after the latest round of coalition talks with the Labour Party.
Asked if the reports would have a big impact, he said: "Yes, we have sought information that would have a bearing on discussions. Important information."
Peters said on Tuesday that his party believed the economy to be in a worse state than the conservative National Party government was arguing before last month's general election.
He said it was seeking "the absolute up-to-date position currently from independent sources other than Treasury". Peters has not disclosed the identity of his advisers.
NZ First, which holds the balance of power, is negotiating with both the caretaker National government and centre-left Labour over coalition possibilities.

Peters said before the election he would go into coalition with any party that would deliver on 95 percent of his party's policies. Asked if he would achieve that target, he said: "You'll have to wait and see. We will do very well."

Asked if he would be prepared to compromise on his party's compulsory superannuation policy in return for another form of long-term savings strategy, Peters said: "In all topics you have to be prepared to give a little to actually gain a lot. We have approached each subject that way. You cannot expect to go into talks and get everything you want."
Asked how an accommodation would be reached with the left-wing Alliance if NZ First formed a coalition with Labour, Peters said: "It's an issue Labour will have to resolve."
Asked if he meant that Labour would have to "deliver" the Alliance's support, he said: "I think I have said that from day one."
Labour, with 37 seats, and NZ First, with 17, would need the support of the Alliance's 13 members of parliament to command a majority in the 120-seat house.
